title: Agentic Ai: Practice Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say exponential backoff alone is not enough, and that jitter is required as well?
options: Jitter makes the retry loop faster by removing the delay
Every client that saw a failure at the same instant computes the same backoff delay and retries at the same instant, re-creating the overload spike, so randomizing the waits spreads them out
Jitter converts a transient failure into a permanent one so the circuit breaker can trip earlier
Jitter guarantees the Retry-After header is always honored even when it is absent
questions.explanation: The lesson: exponential backoff alone has the flaw that clients synchronized to the same failure compute the same delay and retry simultaneously, re-creating the spike. Jitter randomizes each wait, spreading retries across the window.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance on a review board?
options: A review board should approve every AI use so no decision escapes oversight.
A review board should not approve every AI use, should not replace system owners, and should produce decisions, owners, deadlines, and records rather than only discussing risk.
A review board should be made up only of technologists so technical risk is fully understood.
A review board should replace the people who build, buy, own, and operate each AI system.
questions.explanation: The lesson gives three disciplines that keep a review board from becoming theater: it should not approve every AI use (that creates a bottleneck), it should not replace system owners (a named person stays accountable for each system), and a useful meeting produces decisions, owners, deadlines, and records rather than only discussing risk. A committee made of a single discipline, and a committee that does the building and owning, are presented as failures.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Frameworks overview - LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK”, what is the central focus?
options: By now you can build a single agent: a model, a loop, some tools. The hard part is deciding what holds the pieces together when the work grows.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: By now you can build a single agent: a model, a loop, some tools. The hard part is deciding what holds the pieces together when the work grows. This lesson surveys the five frameworks you will actually meet in the wild, and it is honest about what each one is for. LangChain is an integration ecosystem. LangGraph is a stateful graph runtime for workflows that branch and loop. CrewAI is a role-based layer for teams of agents with jobs and backstories. The OpenAI Agents SDK is a deliberately tiny set of primitives with clean handoffs and guardrails. The Claude Agent SDK gives the agent a computer with built-in file, shell, and edit tools. You will learn the mental model behind each one, see the same small task written in two of them so the difference is concrete, and finish with a decision path for choosing a framework instead of trusting star counts.

questions.question: What cost discipline does the lesson say keeps an eval quality gate from being switched off?
options: Run the full LLM-as-judge suite on every commit to catch regressions early
Use cheap code-based graders in CI on every commit and reserve expensive LLM-as-judge evaluations for preview and production
Run no automated evals and rely on manual review of a few prompts before each release
Run expensive evals only on Fridays so the bill stays low
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that a gate costing real money on every commit gets switched off the first month, so it wires the cheap code-based layers into every-commit CI and reserves the expensive judges for preview and production evaluation.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Compliance: Data Residency, Audit Logging, and Retention for AI Systems”, what is the central focus?
options: Security controls who can act. Compliance is the record of what that actor did with other people's data, and it lives in three separate controls. Data residency decides where the data is stored and processed and how it may cross borders.
A history of the technology and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Security controls who can act. Compliance is the record of what that actor did with other people's data, and it lives in three separate controls. Data residency decides where the data is stored and processed and how it may cross borders. Audit logging keeps an immutable record of what happened, per action, so a regulator or an investigator can reconstruct it later. Retention puts a clock on how long you keep any of it. This lesson reads the EU AI Act's record-keeping article and GDPR's storage-limitation principle, then shows how a real agent pipeline turns its own event stream into an auditable trail.

questions.question: How does the lesson say a capability eval becomes a regression eval?
options: A capability eval is deleted as soon as it passes so the suite stays small
A capability eval is refreshed from new production output each quarter
A capability eval that hits a persistently high pass rate graduates into the regression suite, where it starts measuring whether the behavior still works reliably
A capability eval is run only by human graders once it passes
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the self-healing structure: once an eval hits a persistently high pass rate it graduates from asking can we do this at all to asking can we still do this reliably, so nothing already proven can quietly regress.

questions.question: The lesson says a backup can meet the database RPO and still fail the retrieval RPO. What does that mean?
options: The database restore succeeded but the indexes were rebuilt with different ANN parameters
Rows were restored cleanly, but the retrieval system was not restored to a known semantic state, so search returns old chunks or mixes embedding model versions
The physical backup was taken before the last write was committed
The restore ran faster than the recovery time objective allowed
questions.explanation: The lesson's example: you restore the database cleanly, the application comes back, but support search returns old policy chunks and mixes two embedding model versions in the same result set. The backup met the database recovery point but failed the retrieval recovery point.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Evaluation: Evals, Golden Datasets, LLM-as-Judge, and When It Lies”, what is the central focus?
options: An agent you cannot measure is an agent you cannot trust, and the moment a model changes you have no way to know what you traded away.

questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: An agent you cannot measure is an agent you cannot trust, and the moment a model changes you have no way to know what you traded away. This lesson walks the evaluation stack from the bottom up: the golden dataset that anchors everything, the classic metrics that break on open-ended output, the LLM-as-judge technique that replaces them, and the biases that make a judge lie, from position and verbosity preference to rating its own output too high and being misled by a confident wrong answer.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Case Study: Workflow Automation Agents (Browsers, Clicks, and Typing)", what is the one idea to carry out?
options: The model's reasoning rarely fails: grounding fails when the click lands on the wrong element, and blast radius is underestimated when the click submits something real, and both are engineering problems solved before production
Better prompting is the main fix for click accuracy
Screenshots are the only reliable way for an agent to observe a page
Rules-based automation should be replaced entirely by agents
questions.explanation: The lesson states plainly that both failure modes in this class are engineering problems rather than prompting problems, and that both get solved before the agent ever runs in production.

questions.question: How does the lesson say you should build a progress step list from an agent framework's event stream?
options: Render raw tool arguments and private reasoning as the visible steps
Mark the run done as soon as the last visible token lands
Fake a percentage when the loop has no fixed step count
Use per-item events such as tool_called and tool_output, because a tool call is a unit a human can understand while a token is not
questions.explanation: The lesson points to per-item stream events like tool_called, tool_output, and message_output_created as the level to render a step list from, and warns against showing raw tool JSON or reasoning.

questions.question: Per the lesson \"Performance: Latency Budgets, Streaming, Batching, and Speculative Execution\", what is the one idea to carry out?

Time to first token is the only latency metric that matters for every agent
Batching should be the first lever applied to every request, including single interactive ones
questions.explanation: The lesson frames latency as an allocation problem: set the budget from the consumer, measure the number that binds for that consumer, and apply the levers to the step that is over target.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support about model risk management?
options: After the April 2026 replacement of SR 11-7 by SR 26-2, generative and agentic AI are carved out of supervisory scope, but the core discipline of inventory, tiering, independent validation, and ongoing monitoring still applies and must cover AI systems as models.
The US stopped requiring model risk management entirely in 2011, so AI systems no longer need any validation.
Model risk management applies only to banks and is irrelevant to how an enterprise decides which agents to run.
A model only needs to be validated once at launch and then requires no further monitoring because its risk profile never changes.
questions.explanation: The lesson confirms the April 2026 rescission of SR 11-7 in favor of SR 26-2 and notes that generative and agentic AI are excluded from the new guidance's scope, which means the hardest class of model must be governed by judgment for now. It then states the transferable core still holds for AI: inventory every system, tier by damage, validate high-risk systems independently, and monitor after deployment, since a model's risk profile changes as the world it operates in changes.

questions.question: How does the lesson define an integration test for an agent?

A test that runs the whole agent loop against controlled tool side effects, asserting the sequence and outcome, such as the right tool called with the right arguments in the right order

A test that measures cost per request under load
questions.explanation: The lesson defines integration tests as running the whole loop with mocked tools that return fixed data, so the assertion is on tool selection, argument formation, ordering, and that nothing destructive happened.

questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that the goal is not full automation of everything: the agent resolves the easy cases end to end and escalates the hard ones to a person with full context.

questions.question: What is the precise difference, as stated in the lesson, between a dead provider behind an OPEN circuit breaker versus one without it?
options: With a circuit breaker open, the provider is removed from the rate limiter, so quotas are never exhausted
An open circuit makes retries faster by doubling their frequency until the provider recovers
An open circuit means requests are buffered until the cooldown elapses instead of being rejected
A dead provider costs one fast rejection per request instead of one full timeout, which is the difference between a clean failover and a cascading slowdown
questions.explanation: The lesson cites this as the whole value of the open state: requests fail immediately (skip to fallback) without waiting out a full timeout, so a dead provider costs a fast rejection rather than a full timeout per request, separating a clean failover from a cascade.

questions.question: The lesson says that context turns a neutral value into personal data. Which example does it give?

An email address is only personal data when a name appears right next to it
A customer ID is never personal data because it is a random string
Names and phone numbers are the only categories that count as personal data
questions.explanation: Lesson 50 makes the point explicitly: a customer ID looks like a random string on its own, but the moment the agent assembles the account record it points to, the combination relates to a person, so recognition must happen across assembled context, not field by field.

questions.question: Why does the lesson grow the ticket triager into a ticket resolver?

Because classification requires a larger model than resolution does
questions.explanation: The lesson says classification alone is not work a human would hand an agent, so the resolver reads the issue, looks up the account and order, checks the refund policy, and drafts a reply a contact center could actually send.

questions.explanation: The lesson quotes the docs describing the harness as the layer providing tools, context management, and execution environment, and adds that tools are what make the model agentic and the tool surface is where capability is extended.

questions.explanation: The lesson is centered on: Lesson 21 ended on a quiet note: sometimes you don't need a framework at all. This lesson makes that concrete. You write the loop yourself, in roughly a hundred lines, with nothing but an LLM API and a while loop. You see the canonical agent loop in real code, you build a working agent with two tools, you learn the one ordering mistake that trips up every beginner, and you find out exactly where a hand-rolled loop runs out of room and a framework starts to earn its complexity.

questions.question: Which architecture does the lesson describe for the research system?
options: A single agent with one web search tool looping until it stops
A fixed workflow over a predefined list of sources
An orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates specialized subagents that run in parallel with their own context windows and search tasks
A debate between two agents that argue until they agree
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the shipped system as a lead researcher coordinating specialized subagents that run in parallel, each with its own context window and search task.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say a RAG pipeline must normalize data before it reaches the embedding model?
options: Because normalization is a nice-to-have that only matters for very large corpora
Because raw payloads contain structure and noise that waste the embedding token budget, dilute attention with recurring system strings, and produce low-quality vectors that retrieve poorly
Because normalization replaces the need for chunking entirely
Because the embedding model can automatically separate signal from syntax on its own
questions.explanation: The lesson states that raw SaaS JSON and raw HTML are hostile to vector retrieval: embedding them wastes tokens on structural syntax, causes the model to assign weight to recurring system strings instead of meaning, and yields low-quality vectors.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Scaling Agent Workloads: Horizontal Scaling, Queues, and Worker Pools", why does a worker need to be stateless for horizontal scaling to work?
options: Stateless workers are the only kind that can call a model provider
If each request's context lives in the worker's memory, only that worker can finish it, so adding workers does not spread the work
Stateless workers avoid consuming any CPU or memory while idle
State is an anti-pattern in all distributed systems
questions.explanation: The lesson states that for horizontal scaling to work, state must live somewhere addressable by any worker, so any copy can pick the work up. Context held in one worker's memory makes it the only one able to finish the request.
